content: Syringomas are benign tumors originating from the eccrine sweat ducts, most commonly appearing as small, skin-colored or yellowish papules on the lower eyelids and upper cheeks. These lesions can also occur in other areas, such as the axillae, chest, abdomen, neck, scalp, groin, penis, or vulva. They are typically symmetrical, multiple, and may cluster together. Syringomas are adnexal neoplasms composed of well-differentiated ductal structures. The term syringoma is derived from the Greek word syrinx, meaning pipe or tube, reflecting the tubular structures seen in these tumors. Syringomas can be classified into four subtypes based on Friedman and Butler's classification: localized, associated with Down syndrome, generalized (including eruptive syringomas), and familial forms. The pathogenesis of syringomas remains unclear, but they are thought to result from hyperplastic growths of the intraepidermal portion of eccrine ducts, potentially triggered by inflammatory reactions. Another hypothesis suggests that they may arise from hamartomas of pluripotent stem cells. Hormonal influences may also play a role, as syringomas are more common in females. In some cases, phosphorylase deficiency associated with diabetes mellitus may contribute to the development of clear-cell syringomas due to glycogen accumulation in the skin. Genetically, familial syringomas have been linked to mutations on chromosome 16q22 and are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. These familial cases often present during adolescence or preadolescence and predominantly affect the face. Grossly, syringomas appear as small, firm papules, typically less than 3 mm in diameter. Microscopically, they are characterized by eccrine duct-like structures embedded in a fibrous stroma. Immunohistochemical studies reveal the presence of eccrine enzymes, such as leucine aminopeptidase, succinic dehydrogenase, and phosphorylase, as well as cytokeratin expression patterns indicative of eccrine differentiation. Electron microscopy shows ductal cells with short microvilli, desmosomes, luminal tonofilaments, and lysosomes. Syringomas are associated with certain conditions, including Down syndrome, diabetes mellitus, Hailey-Hailey disease, Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, and Nicolau-Balus syndrome. They are generally sporadic but can also occur in familial forms. When associated with Down syndrome, syringomas are often located in the periorbital region, though eruptive variants have been reported. Differential diagnoses for syringomas include acne vulgaris, apocrine hydrocystoma, basal cell carcinoma, colloid milium, Cowden disease, granuloma annulare, microcystic adnexal carcinoma, milia, sebaceous hyperplasia, steatocystoma multiplex, trichoepithelioma, tuberculosis, and xanthelasma. Syringomas affect approximately 1% of the population, with a higher prevalence in females. They are most commonly observed during puberty but can occur at any age. There is no racial predilection, and no specific risk factors have been identified. Most patients with syringomas are asymptomatic, though some may experience pruritus. Physical examination typically reveals small, skin-colored or yellowish papules, which may appear translucent or cystic. Eruptive syringomas can present as hyperpigmented papules on the chest, penile shaft, or vulva. Diagnosis is primarily clinical but can be confirmed with a skin biopsy. Histopathological examination is essential to differentiate syringomas from other conditions, such as microcystic adnexal carcinoma. There are no specific laboratory or imaging findings associated with syringomas. Treatment is usually sought for cosmetic reasons, as syringomas are benign and asymptomatic. Medical therapies include oral isotretinoin, topical atropine, topical tretinoin, and oral tranilast. Surgical options aim to remove the lesions with minimal scarring and include excision, electrocautery, electrodesiccation and curettage, carbon dioxide laser ablation, Er:YAG laser ablation, cryotherapy, dermabrasion, and trichloroacetic acid application. However, complete removal is often challenging, and recurrence is common due to the dermal embedding of the lesions. Clinical follow-up and consideration of repeat biopsy for persistent or recurrent lesions are recommended. Prognosis is excellent, with most patients experiencing no complications or sequelae. Treatment typically results in minimal scarring and no recurrence.
